nm:technique-schur-block-elimination.why: The statement gives the full goal: M is invertible if and only if S is invertible, with the inverse formula and the reduced solve. I checked the six proof steps by block multiplication and all are correct. The source (mathlib) proves only the LDU identity over a commutative ring. The authored proof derives the rest. No use evidence exists, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. The Schur complement is a basic tool in linear solvers and optimization. The hypothesis that A is invertible limits the use. The proof is short block algebra. The worked application is correct.

review.conditions: The conditions are complete. They state field K, the block sizes and the two-sided inverse of A. The empty-block case is covered.
review.prerequisites: The proof uses only block multiplication and the definition of inverse. No hidden prerequisite exists.
review.alignment: The proof proves the full statement: the iff, the inverse formula and the solve reduction. It matches the source LDU identity.
review.why: Every step is valid. The worked application is correct. I accept this record.

step_reviews.why: Block multiplication gives LH=[[A,0],[C,S]]. Then LHU has bottom-right block CA^-1 B + S = D. The result is M. This is correct.
The two products L L^-1 and U U^-1 are the identity in both orders. They need no inverse of S. This is correct.
H^-1 is diag(A^-1,S^-1). The inverse of a product is the reverse product of inverses. So U^-1 H^-1 L^-1 inverts M. This is correct.
If M is invertible, H=L^-1 M U^-1 is a product of invertible matrices. The bottom-right block of H H^-1 is S J, and of H^-1 H is J S. Both equal I. So S is invertible. This is correct.
I computed U^-1 H^-1 and then its product with L^-1. I got the four stated blocks. This is correct.
Ax+By=f gives x=A^-1(f-By). Substitution into Cx+Dy=g gives Sy=g-CA^-1 f. The steps are reversible, so the two systems are equivalent. This is correct.

computation_reviews.why: A=diag(2,3), so A^-1=diag(1/2,1/3). S=0-(1/2+1/3)=-5/6, and its inverse is -6/5. This is correct.
The three equations give 1, 2 and 0. Uniqueness follows because A and S are invertible. The conclusion is correct.

nm:technique-operator-neumann-series.why: The statement gives the full goal: I-T has a bounded inverse, and the tail and norm bounds hold. I checked the six proof steps and all are valid. The source proves invertibility in a normed ring only. The authored proof adds the quantitative tail estimate. No use evidence exists, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. The theorem supports perturbation theory, integral equations and iterative methods. The condition ||T||<1 is strong but common. The proof needs completeness and the scalar geometric series. The worked Volterra application is correct. I checked ||T||=1/2, the powers T^n 1, the sum 75973/46080 and the 1/64 bound.

review.conditions: The conditions are complete. They state a Banach space, a bounded T with q<1 and N>=0. The cases q=0 and the zero space are covered.
review.prerequisites: The proof uses the scalar geometric series and completeness of E. Both are stated. The FTC prerequisite is for the application only.
review.alignment: The proof proves invertibility, convergence in operator norm, the tail bound and the bound on ||R||. This is the full statement.
review.why: Every step is valid. The worked application is correct. I accept this record.

step_reviews.why: The bound ||UV||<=||U|| ||V|| and induction give ||T^n||<=q^n. The case ||I||<=1 includes the zero space. This is correct.
The triangle inequality and ||T^n||<=q^n bound the difference of partial sums by the geometric tail. The tail tends to 0, so the sums are Cauchy. This is correct.
For each x, P_N x is Cauchy. E is complete, so the limit Rx exists. R is linear as a pointwise limit. The bound ||R x||<=||x||/(1-q) follows. This is correct.
The limit m to infinity in ||(P_m-P_N)x|| gives the tail bound by continuity of the norm. This gives the operator-norm bound and the convergence. This is correct.
(I-T)P_N = I-T^(N+1) by telescoping. ||(I-T)(P_N-R)||<=||I-T|| ||P_N-R|| tends to 0, and ||T^(N+1)|| tends to 0. So (I-T)R=I. The other order is the same. This is correct.
If q=0 then T=0, R=I and all tails are 0. The proof uses only powers of T, so no commutation is needed. This is correct.

computation_reviews.why: For ||u||<=1, |(Tu)(x)|<=x/2<=1/2. The function 1 gives 1/2 at x=1. So ||T||=1/2 on C[0,1] with the sup norm. This is correct.
The integral of t^n/(2^n n!) times 1/2 is x^(n+1)/(2^(n+1)(n+1)!). The induction is correct and uses the antiderivative of a power.
The series of T^n 1 gives the sum of x^n/(2^n n!), which is the power series of exp(x/2). The uniform convergence remarks are correct, although the argument is longer than needed.
The bound is (1/2)^7/(1/2)=1/64 with ||1||=1. The sum of the seven terms at x=1 is (46080+23040+5760+960+120+12+1)/46080 = 75973/46080. This is correct.
(1/2) integral of exp(t/2) from 0 to x is exp(x/2)-1. So u-Tu=1. Uniqueness follows as I-T is invertible. This is correct.

nm:technique-finite-field-gauss-sum.why: The statement gives the full goal: |G|^2=q, and G^2=chi(-1)q for a quadratic chi. I checked the six proof steps and all are valid. The source proves the product identity G(chi,psi)G(chi inverse,psi inverse)=q only. The authored proof is a direct and independent calculation. No use evidence exists, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. Gauss sums are central in number theory and in the theory of exponential sums. The reach in other areas is smaller. The worked application modulo 5 is correct. I checked the characters, the sums S(1) and S(2), and the sign G>0.

review.conditions: The conditions are complete. They state finite F, nontrivial chi and psi, and chi^2=1 for the square formula. The step s6 uses chi(-1)^2=1 correctly.
review.prerequisites: The proof uses only character values on roots of unity and bijections of F. de Moivre is a prerequisite for the application only.
review.alignment: The proof proves |G|^2=q and G^2=chi(-1)q. This is the full statement. It is independent of the source product identity.
review.why: Every step is valid. The worked application is correct. I accept this record.

step_reviews.why: Each value of a character on a finite group is a root of unity. So its modulus is 1 and the conjugate is the inverse. This is correct.
The map x to ax permutes F^x. So the sum S satisfies S=chi(a)S with chi(a) not 1. Hence S=0. This is correct.
The shift x to x+z gives sum psi = 0. For b not 0, y to by permutes F. Removing the term y=0 gives -1. For b=0 the sum is q-1. This is correct.
The terms with x=0 or y=0 vanish because chi(0)=0. For x=ty, chi(x) conj chi(y) = chi(t) and psi(x) conj psi(y) = psi((t-1)y). This is correct.
For t=1 the inner sum is q-1. For t not 1 it is -1. Also the sum of chi(t) over t not 0,1 is -1. So |G|^2 = (q-1)+1 = q. This is correct.
If chi^2=1, the values are +1 or -1. So conj G = chi(-1) G after x to -x. Then q = G conj G = chi(-1) G^2. As chi(-1)^2=1, G^2=chi(-1)q. This is correct.

computation_reviews.why: The powers of 2 modulo 5 are 1,2,4,3 with values 1,-1,1,-1. zeta is a fifth root of unity and is not 1. So psi(t)=zeta^t is a nontrivial additive character. This is correct.
The squares are 0,1,4,4,1. The root count of x^2=t is 1+chi(t) for all t in F, including t=0. The additive sum for a not 0 is 0, so S(a)=sum of chi(t)psi(at). This is correct.
The change t=a^-1 s gives S(a)=chi(a)^-1 G. As chi(a)=+1 or -1, S(1)=G and S(2)=-G. This is correct.
chi(-1)=chi(4)=1, so G^2=5. G=zeta+zeta^4-zeta^2-zeta^3 = 2cos(72 deg)-2cos(144 deg), which is positive. So G=sqrt(5). This is correct.
Direct enumeration gives S(1)=1+2zeta+2zeta^4 and S(2)=1+2zeta^2+2zeta^3. The identity that the fifth roots sum to 0 makes them equal sqrt(5) and -sqrt(5). This is correct.

nm:technique-localization-exactness.why: The statement gives the full goal: localization keeps exact sequences exact. I checked the five proof steps against the fraction relation u(tm-sn)=0 and all are valid. The source proves exactness over a commutative semiring. The authored proof adds the endpoint cases. No use evidence exists, so I judged influence and application from the mathematics. The fact is basic in commutative algebra and algebraic geometry. The conditions are very weak. review.conditions: The conditions are complete. They state a commutative ring R, a multiplicative set S with 1, and R-linear maps. The case 0 in S is covered.
review.prerequisites: The proof uses only the definition of equality of fractions. No hidden prerequisite exists.

step_reviews.why: If u(tm-sn)=0, then u(t f(m)-s f(n))=0 by linearity. So the induced map is well defined. Composition commutes on fractions. This is correct.
gf=0 gives image in kernel. If g(n)/s=0, there is u with u g(n)=0, so g(un)=0. This is correct.
Exactness gives m with f(m)=un. Then (S^-1 f)(m/(us)) = un/(us) = n/s. This proves the reverse inclusion. This is correct.
If f(m)/s=0, then f(um)=0 for some u. Injectivity gives um=0, so m/s=0. For surjective g, a preimage n of p gives n/s mapped to p/s. This is correct.
A short exact sequence means exactness at three places. The steps above cover the middle place and both end places. For 0 in S, all fractions are 0 and all the conclusions hold. This is correct.

computation_reviews.why: Z[1/2] is the localization at the powers of 2. Exactness gives S^-1(Z/6) = Z[1/2]/6Z[1/2]. The ideals (6) and (3) are equal because 2 is a unit. This is correct.
2 is a unit modulo 3 with inverse 2. So a/2^n to a(2^-1)^n is well defined as a ring map. Equivalent fractions have the same image. This is correct.
The map is surjective. Its kernel is the set of fractions with numerator divisible by 3, which is 3Z[1/2]. So the quotient is Z/3. This is correct.
The class of 3 is killed by 2, so it becomes 0. The class of 2 has order 3 in Z/3 and stays nonzero. Inversion of all nonzero integers gives Q/6Q=0. This is correct.

step_reviews.why: The base cases are right and the induction setup is clear. The distinct node case comes first.
The expansion along the last row gives a polynomial of degree at most n-1. The top coefficient is the cofactor with sign plus.
Two equal rows give zero. Pairing each permutation term with its row swap gives opposite signs and equal values, so they cancel.
The identity for X^k-a^k gives the factor theorem. The nodes are distinct, so the earlier factors are nonzero at a later root.
A polynomial of degree at most n-1 with n-1 distinct roots is its top coefficient times the product. Substituting the last node gives the formula. The repeated node case gives zero on both sides.
The adjugate identity is correct. A zero determinant means a repeated node and two equal rows, so V is not onto. The system Vc=y then gives one solution for distinct nodes.

computation_reviews.why: The product 1*2*4*1*3*2 is 48, which is not zero. I checked it in Python. The conclusion of unique solvability is right.
The Lagrange basis has nonzero denominators for distinct nodes. Direct substitution gives the delta property.
The nodes and data are copied correctly. The three basis terms have the right constants -1/8, -1/4 and 1/24. I checked them in Python.
The expansion equals x^3-2x^2+1, which I checked in Python. The values at 0,1,2,4 are 1,0,1,33. Uniqueness follows from the determinant.

step_reviews.why: A*A is Hermitian and v*A*Av equals the square of the norm of Av, so it is positive semidefinite. The spectral theorem applies.
The inner product of u_i and u_j equals delta_ij by the stated calculation, because lambda_j equals sigma_j squared. The vectors are orthonormal.
For i above p the norm of Av_i is zero. The range is the span of the u_i, with dimension p, so p equals r.
Gram-Schmidt extension to an orthonormal basis is valid. The remainder is nonzero because the vector lies outside the span.
U and V have orthonormal columns, so they are unitary. The relations A v_i = sigma_i u_i give U*AV = Sigma and then A = U Sigma V*.
The norm squared of Ax is the weighted sum of the |c_i|^2, which is at most sigma_1^2 times the norm squared of x. Equality holds at v_1. The case r=0 is correct.

computation_reviews.why: A*A is [[1,1],[1,2]], the characteristic polynomial is lambda^2-3lambda+1 and the roots are (3+-sqrt5)/2, both positive. This is correct.
phi^2 equals (3+sqrt5)/2 and phi^-2 equals (3-sqrt5)/2. So the singular values are phi and 1/phi. I checked the numbers in Python.
The vector (1,lambda-1) solves the eigen equation. The left vector A v equals (lambda,lambda-1,0) with the right norm. The formulas are correct.
The two left vectors span the first two coordinates and (0,0,1) completes U. The extremal amplifications are phi and 1/phi.
The ratio phi/(1/phi) equals phi^2, about 2.618, which I checked in Python. The remark on the block determinant is correct.

nm:technique-gaussian-quadratic-integral.why: The statement is complete and the mathematics is correct. The one source is a scalar mathlib theorem. No use evidence exists, so influence and application come from the mathematics. The result gives the full normalization for all positive definite A and all b. review.conditions: The hypotheses cover A real symmetric positive definite and b any real vector. The proof uses them in steps s3 and s4.

step_reviews.why: The tail bound exp(-t^2) at most exp(-|t|) is true for |t| at least 1. Tonelli applies to a nonnegative integrand.
Polar coordinates give 2 pi times 1/2, which is pi. J is above 0, so J is the root of pi. The scaling gives the root of 2 pi over lambda.
The spectral theorem gives A equal Q Lambda Q transpose. Each eigenvalue is q^T A q, which is above 0. The determinant is the product.
I expanded the product. The cross terms equal -2 b^T x because A is symmetric. The new exponent equals the old one.
The map x equal mu plus Q y has Jacobian 1. Then (x-mu)^T A (x-mu) equals y^T Lambda y. The step does not write this identity but it is immediate.
Tonelli splits the integral into d scalar integrals. The product of the roots of 2 pi over lambda_i equals (2 pi)^(d/2) over the root of det A. All factors are finite and above 0.

computation_reviews.why: A equals [[2,1],[1,2]] and b equals (1,0). The determinant is 3. The inverse is (1/3)[[2,-1],[-1,2]]. So mu equals (2/3,-1/3). The step does not state A, but the values are correct.
b^T A^-1 b equals 2/3, so the factor is exp(1/3). With d equal 2, Z equals 2 pi exp(1/3) over the root of 3. The calculation is correct.
Division by Z gives a density. The shift y equal x-mu gives the exponent -y^T A y/2. The theorem gives the total 1.

The eigenvalues are 1 and 3 with the stated eigenvectors. The variances are 1 and 1/3. The rotation gives [[2/3,-1/3],[-1/3,2/3]]. The integration by parts is correct. The mean mu follows from the shift.

nm:technique-beta-gamma-integral.why: The statement is complete and the proof is correct for real a and b above 0. The source is a mathlib theorem for complex parameters. step_reviews.why: The integral near 0 equals at most 1/a. For t at least 1 the bound by C exp(-t/2) holds with a finite maximum. The case a at most 1 gives C equal 1.
Each factor that is not a singular power is bounded on its half interval. So B is finite. The Gamma integrand is above 0 on (1,2), so Gamma(a+b) is above 0.
The integrand is nonnegative. So Tonelli gives the product of two integrals as the integral over the quadrant.
The map (r,s) to (rs, r(1-s)) is a smooth bijection onto the quadrant. Its Jacobian has absolute value r. The new integrand is correct.
The integrand is a product of a function of r and a function of s. Tonelli splits it. Gamma(a+b) is above 0, so division is valid.
With s equal x/(1+x), 1+x equals 1/(1-s). The powers combine to s^(a-1)(1-s)^(b-1) ds. The map is a bijection from (0,infinity) to (0,1).

computation_reviews.why: The powers give a equal 3/2 and b equal 5/2, so a+b equals 4. The step does not state this match, but the result is correct.
Integration by parts gives Gamma(t+1) equal t Gamma(t). The boundary term goes to 0 at both ends for t above 0. Gamma(1) equals 1.
The substitution u equal v^2 gives Gamma(1/2) equal 2 times the half-line Gaussian integral, which is the root of pi. So Gamma(3/2) equals root pi over 2 and Gamma(5/2) equals 3 root pi over 4.
Gamma(4) equals 6. The value is (root pi/2)(3 root pi/4)/6, which equals 3 pi/8 over 6, which is pi/16. The calculation is correct.

nm:technique-hermite-gaussian-orthogonal.why: The statement is complete and the proof is correct for all m and n at or above 0. The source proves only the derivative identity, not the orthogonality. The authored proof adds the integration by parts and the boundary limits. No use evidence exists, so influence and application come from the mathematics. The result supports least-squares projection and control variates. The proof uses a few elementary steps and one earlier integral. The worked application is a short direct calculation.

review.conditions: The proof uses integer m and n at or above 0 and the weight exp(-x^2/2). Boundary terms vanish by the decay in s3.
review.prerequisites: The proof uses integration by parts and the Gaussian integral. Both are listed and used correctly.
review.alignment: The proof gives the value for m equal n, zero for m not equal n, and absolute convergence. It matches the scope.
review.why: Every proof step is valid. The recurrence, the derivative formula and the boundary terms are correct. The worked application is correct.

step_reviews.why: By induction x H_n is monic of degree n+1. The derivative has lower degree. So H_(n+1) is monic.
The product rule gives D((-1)^n H_n phi) equal (-1)^n (H_n' - x H_n) phi. This equals (-1)^(n+1) H_(n+1) phi.
For large |x|, k log|x| is at most x^2/4. So |x|^k exp(-x^2/2) is at most exp(-x^2/4), which is integrable. This also gives the limit 0.
Each boundary term is a polynomial times phi, so it goes to 0. The integration by parts n times is valid on finite intervals. The two signs (-1)^n cancel.
If n is above m, the nth derivative of H_m is 0. If n equals m, the nth derivative is n! because H_n is monic. The Gaussian integral gives the root of 2 pi.
The integrand is symmetric in m and n. So the case n below m follows from the case n above m.

computation_reviews.why: H1 is x, H2 is x^2-1, H3 is x^3-3x and H4 is x^4-6x^2+3. So x^4 equals H4+6 H2+3 H0. This is correct.
The residual is H4+(6-b)H2+(3-a)H0. Under the standard normal law the norms squared are n!. The sum is correct.
The sum of squares has its unique minimum at a equal 3 and b equal 6. The minimum value is 24.
E[X^4] equals 3. The norm squared is 24+36*2+9, which is 105. So the variance is 105-9, which is 96.
X^4-6(X^2-1) equals H4+3. Its mean is 3 and its variance is 4!, which is 24. The reduction from 96 to 24 is correct.

nm:technique-lagrange-multipliers.why: The result gives the full first-order rule for equality constraints. The mathlib source is a Banach space version, and the authored proof is for C1 maps on R^n. The normal form needs independent constraint gradients. The proof uses the inverse function theorem. An application needs a system of equations. Use scores come from the mathematics.

review.conditions: The conditions are complete: C1 maps, an open set, m at most n and a local extremum on S. The normal form uses independent gradients, as the statement says.

review.why: I checked each step. The rank count, the extension map L, the curve of points in S and the sign change at the extremum are valid. The worked example checks pass by hand and by Python.

step_reviews.why: The row relation is exactly the claimed relation, so linear dependence of the rows is enough.
Independent rows give rank m+1 and a kernel of dimension n-m-1. The map x to (Jx,Lx) is injective between spaces of equal dimension, so it is bijective.
The map G-hat is C1 with an invertible derivative at x0. The inverse function theorem gives local C1 inverse maps. The cited result is in the packet.
The point y_t lies in the open set W for small t. The inverse image x_t has f(x_t)=f(x0), so it lies in S, and phi(x_t)=phi(x0)+t.
The inverse is continuous, so x_t tends to x0. Points of S near x0 with phi above and below phi(x0) contradict a local extremum.
If lambda0 were zero, the relation would be a nontrivial relation among independent gradients. So lambda0 is not zero, and division gives the normal form.

computation_reviews.why: The setup is correct: n=3, m=1, and the gradient of f has length 2 on S. The gradient of phi is (y,x+z,y). The equations are right.
If y = 0 and mu is not zero, then x = z = 0, which is not on the sphere. So mu = 0 and x+z = 0, and phi = 0. This is correct.
If y is not zero then mu is not zero and x = z = y/(2mu). The middle equation gives mu^2 = 1/2. This is correct.
The constraint gives 2y^2 = 1, so y = +-1/sqrt2 and x = z = +-1/2. The value at the point is sqrt2/2. I checked it in Python.
For mu = -1/sqrt2 the points are +-(-1/2,1/sqrt2,-1/2) and the value is -sqrt2/2. I checked it in Python.
The sphere is compact, so the extrema are critical values. The matrix has eigenvalues 0 and +-1/sqrt2, which I checked. The answer agrees.

nm:technique-gauss-lemma-primitive-polyn.why: The statement is complete and the proof is correct. The source proves only the product of primitive polynomials over a GCD domain. The authored proof adds the irreducibility transfer and the modulo p test. No use evidence exists, so influence and application come from the mathematics. The result is a base tool for number fields and polynomial factorization. The proof needs only elementary ring facts. The worked examples are correct. The last step of the application has a self-contradicting remark, which the author should clean.

review.conditions: Parts (1) and (2) use primitive polynomials. Part (3) uses a monic polynomial, which keeps the degree after reduction.
review.prerequisites: No result is listed as a prerequisite. The proof is self-contained apart from the facts that F_p[x] is a domain and that units of Z[x] are plus or minus 1.
review.alignment: The proof covers all 3 parts. It matches the scope.
review.why: Every proof step is valid. The worked application is correct. The note in step s8 says a root test was done and not done. The author should remove it.

step_reviews.why: The reduction map is a ring homomorphism and F_p[x] is a domain. So a prime that divides all coefficients of fg divides all of f or all of g.
A constant primitive polynomial is plus or minus 1, a unit. So f has degree at least 1. A factorization in Q[x] with non-unit factors has factors of degree at least 1.
Each rational polynomial is a rational multiple of a primitive integer polynomial. Part (1) shows that G1 H1 is primitive.
From v f equal u G1 H1 and gcd(v,u) equal 1, v divides all coefficients of G1 H1, so v is 1. Then u divides all coefficients of f, so u is plus or minus 1.
The units of Z[x] are plus and minus 1. G1 and H1 have degree at least 1, so they are not units. This contradicts irreducibility in Z[x].
A factorization in Z[x] is a factorization in Q[x]. The unit factor is a nonzero integer constant that divides all coefficients. Primitivity gives plus or minus 1.
A monic polynomial is primitive. The leading coefficients of a factorization in Z[x] multiply to 1, so a sign change makes both factors monic. Part (2) transfers the result.
A monic non-unit has degree at least 1. The degrees stay after reduction. So the reduced polynomial has a proper factorization, which is a contradiction.

computation_reviews.why: -3 and -1 are 1 modulo 2. So f-bar equals x^3+x+1.
f-bar(0) equals 1 and f-bar(1) equals 3, which is 1 modulo 2. So there is no root.
A proper factorization of a cubic has a degree 1 factor, so it has a root. There is none, so f-bar is irreducible.

The worked example finds x^4 - 10x^2 + 1 for sqrt2 + sqrt3 and I checked the matrix and the polynomial. No use evidence exists, so influence and application scores come from the mathematics.

review.conditions: The hypotheses are bN in N and either 1 in N or N faithful. Both cases are used in s4.
review.prerequisites: The proof lists no result prerequisite. It needs only the adjugate identity over a commutative ring.
review.alignment: The proof gives a monic polynomial for b and then sums and products. This matches the statement.
review.why: I checked all six steps. The adjugate argument and the monic polynomial are correct. The module in s6 contains 1 and is stable under a and b.

step_reviews.why: The module is stable under b, so each b*n_i is an A-combination of the generators. The matrix M has entries in A.
The k equations b*n_i = sum m_ij n_j are the vector equation (bI - M)v = 0. The step is correct.
adj(X)X = det(X)I holds over a commutative ring. Multiplying by the adjugate gives D*n_j = 0 for all j.
D kills every generator, so D kills every A-combination. Then D = D*1 = 0 when 1 is in N, or D = 0 by faithfulness. Both cases are correct.
The determinant det(xI - M) is monic of degree k with coefficients in A. Evaluation at b commutes with the determinant, so chi(b) = D = 0.
The module spanned by a^i b^j is finitely generated and contains 1. The monic equations show that a and b map it into itself. So a+b and ab satisfy the hypotheses.

computation_reviews.why: The four products are alpha*1, alpha*sqrt6, alpha*sqrt2 and alpha*sqrt3. I computed each one and each is an integer combination of the basis.
The rows [0,0,1,1], [0,0,3,2], [2,1,0,0], [3,1,0,0] follow from s1. The block form with P and Q is correct.
The lower left block commutes with the scalar block, so det = det(x^2 I - PQ). I computed PQ = [[5,2],[12,5]] with trace 10 and determinant 1.
The 2 by 2 formula gives y^2 - 10y + 1 with y = x^2. So the polynomial is x^4 - 10x^2 + 1. This is correct.
alpha^2 = 5 + 2 sqrt6, so (alpha^2 - 5)^2 = 24. This gives alpha^4 - 10 alpha^2 + 1 = 0. The check is correct.

nm:technique-nilradical-intersection-of-.why: The source (Lean declaration nilradical_eq_sInf) proves the statement for a commutative semiring. No use record exists. I judged influence and application from the mathematics. The result links nilpotents and prime ideals. Algebraic geometry uses it. It holds in every commutative ring. The proof needs Zorn lemma (nl:1475). The proof is correct. The general form follows by passing to R/I, which is standard but brief. The listed concept prerequisites (polynomial, quotient group) do not fit. Ideal and quotient ring fit better. The application arithmetic is correct.

review.conditions: A commutative ring with 1 is used. The zero ring is fine with the empty intersection equal to R. The general form for an ideal I follows from R/I.
review.prerequisites: The proof uses Zorn lemma (nl:1475) in step s4. The set of ideals is not empty and chains have upper bounds.
review.alignment: The source proves the nilradical equals the infimum of the prime ideals. The authored proof matches it.
review.why: Steps s1 to s8 are valid. Step s8 uses the correspondence of primes of R/I with primes that contain I. This is standard but brief. The application arithmetic in Z/360 is correct.

step_reviews.why: If x^n is in P and P is prime, induction on n gives x in P.
x is not nilpotent, so no power of x is 0. So 0 is not in S.
(0) does not meet S by step s2. So the set of ideals that miss S is not empty.
A union of a chain of ideals is an ideal. It misses S. Zorn lemma (nl:1475) gives a maximal element.
If 1 were in P, then x would be in P, but x is in S and P misses S. So P is proper. The written reason is loose but valid.
P + (a) is an ideal bigger than P, so it is not in the set. So it meets S. The same holds for b. The equations are correct.
The product of the two equations gives x^(m+k) in P + (ab). If ab were in P, x^(m+k) would be in P. This is a contradiction. So P is prime.

x is not in P, so x is not in the intersection of all primes. This gives one inclusion. The general form uses the standard correspondence of primes of R/I with primes that contain I. The step is brief.

computation_reviews.why: The primes of Z/360 match the primes 2, 3, 5 of 360. The ideals (2), (3), (5) have 360/2 = 180, 120 and 72 elements. This is correct.
The intersection is the set of multiples of lcm(2,3,5) = 30. It has 360/30 = 12 elements. This is correct.
x is nilpotent mod 360 exactly when 2, 3 and 5 divide x. So there are 12 nilpotent elements, the multiples of 30. The computer claim is correct.
Steps s2 and s3 give the same set. This agrees with the theorem. The conclusion is correct.

nm:technique-euler-trail-criterion.why: The packet has no use evidence. I judged influence and application from the mathematics. The source proves only the counting lemma and necessity. I checked the authored proof of sufficiency and the example graphs by hand and by computer. All are correct.

step_reviews.why: Each edge of a trail has two different ends, because there are no loops. The count of positions gives 2 times inner visits plus the ends equal to w.
In an Euler trail every edge at w is in the trail. The lemma then gives the parity of each degree for closed and open trails.
A longest trail exists because the graph is finite. If its ends differ, the end b has an odd count in the trail but an even degree, so an unused edge exists.
A walk from a to an end of the unused edge exists by connection. Its first edge outside W starts at a vertex of W.
A closed trail can start at any of its vertices. Appending the unused edge f gives a longer trail, so W was not longest.
The new vertex z makes all degrees even and keeps the graph in one component. The circuit of part (a) gives the trail from u to v after z is removed.

computation_reviews.why: All degrees of K5 are 4. The listed circuit has 10 distinct edges, which are all edges of K5. I checked this by computer.
K4 has four vertices of degree 3. The count of odd vertices is 4, so no Euler trail exists.
The grid has 4 corners of degree 2, 4 midpoints of degree 3 and a center of degree 4. Four odd vertices means no Euler trail.
The degrees are correct: 3, 3, 2, 2 and 2. Only vertices 0 and 1 are odd, so part (b) gives a trail from 0 to 1.
The trail 0,4,1,2,3,0,1 uses the 6 distinct edges of the house graph. It starts at 0 and ends at 1.
The remark is correct and honest. It says the record does not prove Hierholzer's method, and the trails were checked directly.

step_reviews.why: The inverse of I+cEij is I-cEij because Eij squared is zero for i not equal to j. So the claim M=LDR is the same as L^-1 M R^-1 = D.
The induction on n is set up correctly. The base case n=1 is diagonal. The case M=0 is handled in step s6.
If M1j is zero, adding row i gives M1j = Mij which is nonzero, and i is not 1. If M11 is zero, adding column j gives M11 = M1j which is nonzero. All cases are covered.
Adding -(Mi1/p) times row 1 to row i is a transvection and it makes the entry in row i of column 1 zero.
Column 1 is (p,0,...,0), so the column operations do not change rows 2 to n. They clear the first row. The result is diag(p,N).
The factorization of diag(p,N) is correct. The extension of transvections by a 1 on the first position is correct. The zero case is handled.
I multiplied the three matrices: w(a) = [[0,a],[-1/a,0]]. Then w(a)w(-1) = diag(a,1/a). The step-wise reduction gives D = Q diag(1,...,1,d1...dn), and det D = det M.
If det M = 1 then D = I. So M is a product of transvections. Transvections have determinant 1, so they lie in SL_n.

computation_reviews.why: Row 1 becomes (1,5,6) and row 2 becomes (0,-2,-1). Both are correct. Both operations are transvections.
The column operations give the first row (1,0,0). N = [[-2,-1],[-8,-5]]. Correct.
Row 3 becomes (0,0,-1). Then column 3 plus (-1/2) column 2 gives (0,0,-1). D = diag(1,-2,-1). Correct.
The operations are 2+1+1 = 4 row operations and 2+1 = 3 column operations. I applied them in exact arithmetic and got diag(1,-2,-1). So M = L D R.

nm:technique-catalan-cycle-lemma.why: The record has no use evidence. I judged influence and application from the mathematics. step_reviews.why: S_0 = 0 and S_(2n+1) = n-(n+1) = -1. The periodic extension gives S_(k+2n+1) = S_k - 1.
The rotation after m has partial sums S_(m+j)-S_m. They are all negative if and only if S_k < S_m for m < k <= m+2n+1.
The last maximum m on 0 to 2n gives S_k < S_m for m < k <= 2n. For the other k, S_k = S_k' - 1 <= S_m - 1 < S_m. This is correct.
The index k'+2n+1 is in the range (m, m+2n+1]. The sums are integers, so S_k' - 1 < S_m gives S_k' <= S_m. So m is the last index of the maximum.
Because gcd(n,n+1)=1, no sequence is a repetition of a shorter block. So all rotations are distinct. Each orbit has one good member. The count is correct.
The first step is -1 because S_1 < 0. The remaining sums S_k+1 are at most 0 and the total is 0. Negation gives a Dyck word. The inverse map is correct.

computation_reviews.why: C(9,4) = 126. I ran the check by computer. Each sequence has exactly one good rotation.
126/9 = 14 and 70/5 = 14. I counted 14 good sequences by computer.
The values 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, 132, 429 are the Catalan numbers. The words for every n mean n = 0 to 7 here. The claim is about this range only.
The partial sums are correct. The last maximum on 0 to 8 is at index 6 with value 0.
The rotation and its partial sums are correct. All nine are negative.
The Dyck word is (+1,-1,+1,-1,+1,+1,-1,-1). Its sums are 1,0,1,0,1,2,1,0. It is UDUDUUDD. Correct.

nm:technique-kst-c4-free-edge-bound.why: The record has one prerequisite result, Jensen's inequality, which has strong use evidence. The source (mathlib) proves only the general double-counting identity for a relation. The bound, the use of Jensen and the bipartite form are authored. I checked all steps and they are correct. The bound is the start of the Zarankiewicz and extremal graph theory (inference). The worked example was checked: the Fano plane has 21 edges, and the maximum for 5 vertices is 6 (computer check of 1024 graphs).

review.conditions: A simple graph is required and stated. The bound on e is real-valued. The bipartite form needs only no 4-cycle.
review.prerequisites: Jensen's inequality is the one result prerequisite. The finite form is a case of it. The use is correct.
review.alignment: The source proves only the double-counting identity. The bound and the use of Jensen are authored. This match is weak but the authored steps are correct.
review.why: All 7 steps are valid. The quadratic and its roots are correct. Step s7 uses the same pair argument as step s3 for the bipartite graph, which holds.

step_reviews.why: Two common neighbors u and v of a and b give the 4-cycle a,u,b,v. A 4-cycle gives such a pair. So the equivalence holds.
For each v there are C(d(v),2) pairs of neighbors. The sum is the number of cherries.
Each pair has at most one common neighbor. So the number of cherries is at most C(n,2).
The function d(d-1)/2 is convex. The finite Jensen inequality with equal weights is valid. The degree sum is 2e.
Dividing by n/2 gives d(d-1) <= n-1. This is the quadratic in the step. It is correct.
The roots are (1 +- sqrt(1+4(n-1)))/2 = (1 +- sqrt(4n-3))/2. The bound on e follows from e = n*d/2.
The count by y is the sum of C(d(y),2). Two vertices of X with two common neighbors in Y give a 4-cycle. So the count is at most C(m,2).

computation_reviews.why: 7 d(d-1)/2 <= 21 gives d(d-1) <= 6, so d <= 3 and e <= 21. Correct.
I checked the 21 pairs of lines. Each pair meets in exactly one point. So the graph has no 4-cycle.
The graph has 21 edges. 7*C(3,2) = 21 = C(7,2). So the bound is attained.
The largest C4-free bipartite graph on 7+7 vertices has 21 edges (Zarankiewicz number). Correct.
There are 2^10 = 1024 graphs. I ran a computer check and the maximum is 6. Two triangles that share a vertex have 6 edges and no 4-cycle.

step_reviews.why: A smaller grid is a subset of the large grid. A point in the small grid is a point in the large one. The reduction is valid.
The polynomial g_i is monic of degree t_i + 1 and it vanishes on S_i. The step also sets up the proof by contradiction correctly.
Division by a monic polynomial in x_i is possible and it does not raise the total degree. It does not raise the degrees in the other variables. So the quotient degree bound holds.
The degree-D part of h_i g_i has x_i exponent at least t_i + 1 in every monomial. The monomial x^t has exponent t_i, so the coefficient of x^t in r equals that in f.
At a grid point f = 0 by assumption and each g_i = 0. So r = f - sum h_i g_i is 0 there. The step is correct.
Induction on n is valid. For a fixed point of the smaller grid, a polynomial of degree at most t_n with t_n + 1 roots is zero. Then each coefficient vanishes on the smaller grid.
By s5 and s6 r is zero, but s4 says its x^t coefficient is not zero. This is a real contradiction, so f does not vanish on the grid.

computation_reviews.why: The size choice for B' is valid since 1 <= p+1-a < b. Then |A'|+|B'|-1 = p. The choice of C with m = a+b-2 and the degree of f are correct.
With t1 = a-1 and t2 = b-1 the top part of f is (x+y)^m. The coefficient of x^(a-1) y^(b-1) is C(m,a-1). The step is correct.
Since m < p, the factorials in C(m,a-1) have no factor p. So the binomial is nonzero modulo p. The step is correct.
The sizes a > t1 and b > t2 satisfy the theorem. The point it gives has x+y in C, so f is zero there. This contradicts f not zero, which gives the bound.
I computed A+B mod 11 and it has 10 elements. The bound is 6 and C(5,2) = 10 is nonzero modulo 11. The step is correct.
The sum of {0,1,2} and {0,1,2,3} is {0,...,5} with 6 elements. This equals a+b-1, so the bound is sharp here.
Here a+b-1 = 6 > 5 and B' has size 3. Then m = 4 and C(4,2) = 6 is 1 modulo 5, so it is nonzero. A'+B' has 5 elements, so |A+B| = 5.

step_reviews.why: The density is positive, so P and P_t have the same null sets. Its mean is M(t)e^{-Lambda(t)}=1, so P_t is a probability law. Division by the density gives the formula.

For |s-t|<=delta/2, e^{sx}<=e^{tx}e^{delta|x|/2}. Also e^{delta|x|}e^{tx}<=e^{(t+delta)x}+e^{(t-delta)x}. So the bound holds with C_k=sup|x|^k e^{-delta|x|/2}, which is finite. The bound is integrable because t+-delta are in I.

M>0, so Lambda'=M'/M=E_t X. The second derivative is M''/M-(M'/M)^2=E_t[X^2]-(E_t X)^2. A variance is not negative, so Lambda is convex.
For t>=0 the events {X>=a} and {e^{tX}>=e^{ta}} are the same. Markov inequality gives the bound e^{-ta}M(t).

nm:technique-second-moment-method.why: The statement is complete. The source is the Chebyshev lemma, which covers only part (b). Parts (a), (c) and (d) come from the authored proof, which I checked. If X=0 then |X-mu|=mu, so {X=0} is in {|X-mu|>=mu}. Chebyshev gives Var X/mu^2. The condition mu>0 is used.
If P(X>0)=0 then X=0 almost surely and mu=0, a contradiction. So q>0. The expansion of the square is correct, and X*1_{X>0}=X because X>=0.

The consequence follows from (b) and (a) when E X_n>0. If the ratio tends to u, the liminf bound 1/(1+u) follows from (a). The step is a remark and is correct.

step_reviews.why: Abel summation with a_n=1 and f(t)=t^(-s) gives N*N^(-s)+s times the integral of floor(t) t^(-s-1). f is C1 for complex s. The sign is correct because f'=-s t^(-s-1).
For Re s>1, N^(1-s) tends to 0. Also floor(t)<=t, so the integral converges absolutely. The limit gives zeta(s)=s times the integral from 1 to infinity.
Both pieces converge for Re s>1. The integral of t^(-s) from 1 to infinity is 1/(s-1), so the first piece is s/(s-1). The formula follows.

step_reviews.why: The chain of powers of a stops. Then a^n(1 - ab) = 0 in a domain gives ab = 1. So R/P is a field and P is maximal. This is valid.
The chain of finite intersections stops. So the intersection of m_1 to m_n is in m_(n+1). This is valid.
A prime that contains the intersection contains a product, so it contains one factor. Two maximal ideals that are comparable are equal. This contradicts distinctness. This is valid.
Primes are maximal and finite in number. Each point is closed. A finite space with all points closed is discrete. This is valid. The listed use of the nilradical result is not needed.
The nilradical is the intersection of the primes. By part (a) these are the maximal ideals. So the nilradical equals J. This is valid.
The chain of powers of J stops. The set of ideals K with K.I nonzero is non empty and has a minimal element by the descending chain condition. This is valid.
By minimality (x) equals K. The ideal xJ has (xJ).I = x J^(n+1) = xI, which is nonzero. So xJ equals K. This is valid.
x = xj gives x(1 - j) = 0. The element 1 - j is a unit, so x = 0. This contradicts xI nonzero. So J^n = 0. This is valid.

computation_reviews.why: 360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5. The primes (2), (3), (5) are maximal and J = (30). This is correct.
30^2 = 900 = 180 mod 360 and 30^3 = 27000 = 75 x 360 = 0. So the index is 3, the largest exponent. This is correct.
720 = 16 x 9 x 5. The powers of 30 mod 720 are 30, 180, 360, 0. So J^3 is not zero and J^4 is zero. The index is 4. This is correct.
The ideal J is (x(x-1)). J^k is zero if and only if x^2 (x-1)^5 divides x^k (x-1)^k, that is k >= 5. The index is 5. This is correct.
The prime (0) of Z is not maximal. The chains (2), (4), (8) and (x), (x^2) never stop. So Z and Q[x] are not Artinian. This is correct.

A monic equation of least degree is used. If a0 is zero, the domain property gives a monic equation of lower degree, or 1 = 0 for degree 1. Both cases fail. The step is complete.
The element a0 is in the ideal of x, so it is in the image of Q prime. A lift in R lies in Q prime and in R, so it is in p. This makes a0 zero, which is a contradiction. The step is valid.
A nonzero x has a0 nonzero and in R bar, which is a field. So a0 is a unit, and x has an inverse. S bar is a field, so Q is maximal.
The inverse of a is integral over R bar. Multiplying the monic equation by a power of a gives the inverse of a in R bar. The ring R bar is not zero. So p is maximal.
Part (a) turns a strict chain of primes of S into a strict chain of primes of R. The chain length is the same. The supremum gives the bound on the dimension.

computation_reviews.why: The norm of 2 + i is 5, so the quotient has 5 elements and is a field. So both ideals are maximal. The element 5 equals the product of 2 + i and 2 - i.
The quotient (3 - 4i)/5 is not in Z[i]. So neither ideal contains the other. The argument by maximal ideals is valid, and it agrees with part (a).
The ring Z[i] mod 5 is F5[x] mod x squared plus 1. The polynomial has roots 2 and -2 mod 5. The Chinese remainder theorem gives F5 times F5 with two maximal ideals. So exactly two primes lie over 5.
The zero ideals contract to the zero ideal, which is not maximal. The ideal 2 + i is maximal and contracts to (5), which is maximal. This agrees with part (b).
Part (c) gives dimension at most 1. The chain zero inside 2 + i has length 1. So the dimension is 1.

The ideal xy - 1 contracts to zero, because a nonzero multiple of it has y degree at least 1. So the chain does not contract to a strict chain. The text does not prove that xy - 1 is prime, but this is a standard fact.
The field Q(x) has a maximal zero ideal. It contracts to the zero ideal of Q[x], which is not maximal. So part (b) fails without integrality.

step_reviews.why: These are the stated properties of Phi_n from the factorization theorem. They are enough here.

Phi_n factors in Z[x] into monic irreducible polynomials. Each one is irreducible in Q[x] by Gauss lemma. The minimal polynomial f is monic and irreducible and divides the product, so it equals one factor. So f is in Z[x].

eta^p is a primitive n-th root because p does not divide n. If g differs from f, they are coprime and both divide x^n-1. Their product divides x^n-1. The quotient is in Z[x] because the divisor is monic.
f divides g(x^p) in Z[x] because f is monic. The Frobenius identity gives g-bar^p = g-bar(x^p). A prime factor pi of f-bar divides g-bar. So pi^2 divides f-bar*g-bar, which divides x^n-1 mod p.
The derivative n*x^(n-1) is not zero mod p and has only the root 0. So x^n-1 and its derivative are coprime. So x^n-1 is squarefree mod p. This contradicts step 4. So g=f.
Each primitive root is zeta^k with gcd(k,n)=1. Write k as a product of primes. None divides n. Repeat step 3 for each prime. So every primitive root is a root of f. So Phi_n divides f and f=Phi_n.

Q(zeta) is the splitting field of x^n-1, so it is Galois of order phi(n). Each automorphism maps zeta to zeta^a and is fixed by a. The composition rule is correct. The text does not say that every sigma_a exists. This follows because zeta^a is a root of the minimal polynomial. The orders are equal, so the map is an isomorphism.

computation_reviews.why: Phi_12 is x^4-x^2+1 and has degree phi(12)=4. The theorem gives irreducibility. So the degree is 4.
The group has the elements 1, 5, 7, 11. The squares 25, 49 and 121 are 1 mod 12. So it is the Klein four-group with three subgroups of order 2.
zeta=sqrt(3)/2+i/2 and zeta^5=-sqrt(3)/2+i/2. Their sum is i. sigma_5 fixes it. The fixed field has degree 2, so it is Q(i).
zeta^2=(1+i*sqrt(3))/2 is fixed by sigma_7 because zeta^14=zeta^2. So the fixed field is Q(sqrt(-3)). The element zeta+zeta^(-1)=sqrt(3) is fixed by conjugation. So that fixed field is Q(sqrt(3)).
V4 has five subgroups. So there are five intermediate fields: Q, Q(i), Q(sqrt(-3)), Q(sqrt(3)) and Q(zeta_12). The conclusion line leaves Q out of the proper subfields. This is a wording fault only.

The terms have one weak sign and their sum is 0, so each term is 0. Thus r(t_i) = 0 at all nodes.

nm:technique-ergodicity-rotation-doublin.why: The entry proves that an irrational rotation and the doubling map are ergodic by Fourier coefficients. step_reviews.why: Parseval gives the norm of f minus the mean as the sum over n not 0 of |f^(n)|^2. This is 0 so f is a constant almost everywhere.
The indicator of an invariant set A is invariant. If it is almost everywhere constant then it is 0 or 1 almost everywhere. So the measure of A is 0 or 1.
Translation invariance gives the rotation case. For D_m the preimage of an interval is |m| intervals of length (b-a)/|m|. The pi-system argument extends this to all Borel sets.
The substitution gives the coefficient e^(2 pi i n alpha) f^(n). For irrational alpha the factor differs from 1 for n not 0. So f^(n)=0 and s1 applies.
The union of q half intervals is mapped to itself by a permutation of the q intervals. It has measure 1/2. So the rational rotation is not ergodic.
U is an isometry by s3 and U e_n=e_(mn). Continuity gives U f as the sum of f^(n) e_(mn). The index map is injective. So f^(mn)=f^(n).
Repeating s6 gives f^(n)=f^(m^j n). The indices are distinct for |m| at least 2. Bessel makes the coefficients square summable so they tend to 0.
Step s7 gives f^(n)=0 for n not 0. Steps s1 and s2 then give that every invariant set has measure 0 or 1. So D_m is ergodic.
